title: The Deeds That Disappeared: City Agrees to $60 Million Settlement Over Homes Taken From Owners
dek: New York City has agreed to a proposed $60 million settlement with residents who lost ownership of their homes through the Third Party Transfer program, ABC7 New York's 7 On Your Side Investigates reported on Oct. 19.
body: Isabel Adon bought into a Bronx co-op on Nelson Avenue in the late 1970s. In 2018, she and dozens of other families in the building stopped being owners. With little or no notice and no payment, they became renters in the apartments they had bought, according to an investigation by ABC7 New York's 7 On Your Side.
> "That was the legacy for my kids." — Isabel Adon
## How a Building Changes Hands

The mechanism was a city program called Third Party Transfer. Under it, New York identifies buildings it considers distressed, meaning they carry physical and financial problems, and transfers the deed to a nonprofit to operate, ABC7 reported. Over roughly three decades and multiple rounds, the city used the process on more than 500 properties.

A City Council investigation found that most of those properties were in minority communities, and that half of the properties selected were not distressed under the legal definition, according to the station.

For the owners, the loss was more than a deed. Residents told ABC7 they saw the transfers as a theft of generational wealth. Junior Gonzalez, a Marine Corps veteran who also bought into the Nelson Avenue building, lost his ownership too.
## Seven Years in Court

In 2019, attorneys Yolande Nicholson and Matthew L. Berman filed a federal lawsuit arguing that the transfers violated the constitutional protection against the government taking private property for public use without just compensation, ABC7 reported. Other law firms later joined the case.

After about seven years of litigation, the city agreed to a proposed $60 million settlement, which ABC7 described as one of the largest local civil rights settlements in recent history. It covers only the hundreds of people affected by the most recent round of transfers, not everyone who lost property under the program. It still needs a judge's approval and sign-off from the residents, and could be resolved by next summer.
Gonzalez was blunt about the deal, telling ABC7 that the plaintiffs are not jumping for joy.
## What Happens to the Program

The city says the program was run under former administrations. A spokesperson for the Department of Housing Preservation and Development told ABC7 that the Mamdani administration and the City Council are working to update and strengthen Third Party Transfer to address the concerns raised in the lawsuits.

The plaintiffs' lawyers want it gone. Berman argued that eminent domain, which requires compensation, is the appropriate tool when the government wants property for policy goals like these, ABC7 reported.
Nicholson told the station she hopes the case and the settlement become a catalyst for change.

For families like Adon's, any check will arrive decades after the purchase and years after the deed left their hands. Whether City Hall keeps a version of the program alive will decide whether other owners face the same letter.

sources.title: Homes 'stolen' from Black and brown residents in New York City: 7 On Your Side Investigates

title: Brick Through the Glass: Hate Crimes Task Force Investigates Attack on Upper East Side Bank
dek: Someone threw a brick through the front window of a Capital One bank on East 86th Street on the morning of Oct. 19 and left graffiti referencing Palestine Action and the Israeli defense company Elbit, police said.
body: The Upper East Side was still waking up at about 7:50 a.m. on Monday, Oct. 19, when someone hurled a brick through the front window of the Capital One bank at 247 East 86th Street, according to ABC7 New York.
Capital One reported damage to multiple glass panels, and the front of the branch had been tagged with red spray paint, the station reported.
## The Message on the Wall

Authorities said the graffiti read "Pal Action" and "Drop Elbit." Palestine Action is an activist movement that protests defense companies linked to Israel, including the Israeli weapons maker Elbit Systems, and activists have previously targeted Capital One over its lending to Elbit, ABC7 reported.

The NYPD's Hate Crimes Task Force took over the investigation. Police had not publicly specified a motive as of the station's report, and no one had been arrested or identified as a suspect. Investigators were canvassing the neighborhood for surveillance video.
No one was hurt.
## Neighbors on Edge
City Council Speaker Julie Menin, who represents the Upper East Side, and other local officials posted about the attack on social media, according to ABC7.

Andrew Kavesh, a neighbor and customer of the bank, told the station the attack was frightening. He said that if it turns out to be a hate crime, particularly one aimed at Jewish people, it would feel deeply personal to him.
> "It's scary." — Andrew Kavesh, Upper East Side resident
## A Rising Count

The attack comes as the NYPD reports a rise in bias crime even as overall crime falls. Through the first nine months of 2026, confirmed hate crimes rose 12.9% citywide, and more than half were anti-Jewish, according to department figures reported by ABC7 on Oct. 7. Over the same period, major crime fell 6.6%.

Whether the Capital One attack is ultimately classified as a hate crime will depend on what investigators determine about who threw the brick and why. As of Monday, investigators had not said whether they believed the attack was connected to earlier protests against the bank.
Anyone with information is asked to call NYPD Crime Stoppers at 1-800-577-TIPS.

sources.title: Hate crime investigation after bank vandalized, windows broken on Upper East Side
NYPD says shootings and murders reached record lows through September

title: Gunman Kills 26-Year-Old on Midtown E Train Platform, Then Escapes on the 7
dek: A 26-year-old Bronx man was shot dead after an argument at the Seventh Avenue-53rd Street station on Oct. 17, and police were still hunting the gunman two days later.
body: The argument began somewhere between the platform and the train. By the time it ended, shortly before 12:30 p.m. on Saturday, Oct. 17, a 26-year-old man from the Bronx lay on the uptown E train platform at the Seventh Avenue-53rd Street station with a gunshot wound to the chest, according to ABC7 New York.

Police said the gunman walked up to the victim, pulled a pistol and fired. Investigators told the station the dispute spilled onto a train and then back onto the platform. The victim was rushed to Bellevue Hospital in critical condition and later died.
## Panic Underground

Riders who were on the platform described terror. A woman performed CPR on the wounded man before emergency crews arrived, ABC7 reported. One witness told the station that people had huddled together when the gunman fired again, and that riders then broke and ran for the stairs.

The shooter did not run far on foot. According to police, he boarded a northbound 7 train and was gone. Investigators were still working to determine whether shots were fired on the platform, on the train, or both.
## 'Not a Random Act'

Police described the killing as targeted. They said it was not a random act and promised they would find the person responsible, ABC7 reported. Sources told the station the two men had been arguing on the platform before the shooting; what started the dispute has not been made public.
The NYPD released surveillance images of the suspect, who was described as wearing red clothing, a black vest and a face mask. As of Monday, Oct. 19, no arrest had been announced.
## A Family Left Waiting

Neighbors told ABC7 the victim worked as a security guard and was a twin; his brother is a Marine stationed in Texas. Relatives and neighbors gathered over the weekend to remember him as detectives canvassed for video along the 7 line.
## Riders on Edge

For riders, the shooting reopened old fears. Commuters told amNY that the killing resurfaced their anxiety about daily conditions underground, describing open drug use, fights, and people in visible mental health crisis on trains and platforms.
NYPD data cited by amNY show subway crime was up 0.9% as of Oct. 1, driven largely by an 11% rise in felony assaults, even as shootings and murders citywide fell to record lows through September.
Police ask anyone with information to call the NYPD Crime Stoppers hotline at 1-800-577-TIPS.

Darryl Rodriguez remembered as police hunt Midtown subway shooter
Subterranean fear: How transit riders say deadly Midtown subway shooting has resurfaced their angst over crime underground

title: Through the Gates: Columbia Students Hand Out Guest Passes to Reopen a Campus Closed for Three Years
dek: Columbia University students set up a 'People's Kiosk' at West 116th Street and Broadway on Oct. 18 and used the school's own guest QR codes to let members of the public onto the Morningside Heights campus.
body: For nearly three years, the wrought-iron gates of Columbia University at West 116th Street and Broadway have marked a hard line between the campus and the city around it. On the evening of Sunday, Oct. 18, a group of students found a way to open them without breaking a single rule, according to amNY.
They called it the People's Kiosk.
## The Loophole

Under Columbia's visitor system, students can generate QR codes that allow guests onto the grounds. Each student can generate five. So the students set up outside the gates and began handing their codes to members of the public, offering what they called friends and family access, amNY reported.

Student Josh Cohen told amNY that dozens of students were participating and that they hoped to bring in as many people as possible. The effort was timed to a night market and performances on campus that evening. Within about 30 minutes, Cohen said, the group had signed in five people, and by later in the evening entire families were walking through the gates.
> "It's unacceptable that the gates have been closed for three years." — Josh Cohen, Columbia student
## How the Gates Closed

Columbia ended general public access in October 2023, when pro-Palestinian protests broke out on campus, amNY reported. By spring 2024, protesters had built a large encampment on the South Lawn. After multiple police raids and years of restrictions, the campus that once functioned as a public crossroads of Morningside Heights has remained closed to anyone without a university ID or an invitation.

In a September statement ahead of the fall semester, President Jennifer Mnookin said the university must protect the safety of its community and preserve the conditions for its academic mission, including reasonable measures to prevent disruption, amNY reported.
## City Hall Leans In

The closure has become a civic fight. Elected officials have rallied outside the gates to demand that the campus reopen, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani has called for a policy change and threatened legal action if the university does not restore public access, according to amNY.

The students' workaround tests how far that access can be stretched from the inside. Whether the university tightens its guest rules in response, or treats the kiosk as a one-night protest, will determine whether the gates at 116th Street stay open a crack or swing shut again.

sources.title: Columbia students find loophole to let public back on campus after three years

title: The Parking Lot War: City Hall Asks Private Owners to Shut ICE Out of Its Staging Grounds
dek: Mayor Zohran Mamdani and more than 100 elected officials sent a letter on Oct. 15 urging private garage and lot owners not to let Immigration and Customs Enforcement use their property for operations.
body: Long before the shots in Marble Hill, residents had been watching the parking lot. For months, constituents reported ICE vehicles gathering at the lot of the Marble Hill Target, the Bronx Times reported. After a federal agent shot a 28-year-old driver nearby on Oct. 8, that lot, and others like it across the city, became the next front in New York's standoff with federal immigration enforcement.
## 'Do Not Rent Your Property to ICE'

On Thursday, Oct. 15, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and more than 100 city and state elected officials sent a letter to private parking garage and lot owners asking them not to rent, lend or otherwise allow ICE to use their property for enforcement, amNY reported.
> "Do not rent your property to ICE." — Mayor Zohran Mamdani

The letter warns that private lots can serve as staging grounds even without any formal agreement, and that each such use gives ICE a launching point for operations, according to amNY. It cites agents using two bank parking lots in Queens and a garage on Morton Street in Manhattan, which removed ICE vehicles after neighbors complained, according to the mayor's office. Officials also received reports of agents operating out of the BJ's Wholesale Club lot in Marble Hill.

Mamdani said city law already bars ICE from using city property as a base of operations. The letter itself is a request, not an enforcement action, and the Bronx Times noted that the city's sanctuary policies generally restrict city agencies and the NYPD, not federal agents on private property.
## Target and Its Landlord

The pressure campaign began before the shooting. On Oct. 5, Bronx and Upper Manhattan officials wrote to Kingsbridge Associates, co-owner of the Marble Hill Target site, asking about its relationship with ICE and urging it to bar agents from the lot, the Bronx Times reported.

Two days after the shooting, Kingsbridge said it had not known ICE was operating on its property and had no working relationship with the agency, according to the office of Council Member Pierina Sanchez. A Target spokesperson said the company has no formal agreement with ICE. Neither company has said whether agents will be kept off the property.

State Sen. Gustavo Rivera urged both companies to ban ICE outright, arguing agents there without permission would be trespassing. At an Oct. 9 rally, he questioned the landlord's claim of ignorance, saying ICE had known about the lot for months, according to amNY.
## Following the Money

Officials are also looking at leverage. City Comptroller Mark Levine sent a letter seeking an independent evaluator to review how the companies handled the situation; city pension funds hold Target investments, the Bronx Times reported. Sanchez said everything is on the table when it comes to limiting city business with developers that work with ICE, and noted that the site's parent company, Washington Square Partners, has received city tax abatements.
Linda Tijani, chair of the city's Commission on Racial Equity, called for pulling city pension money out of Target and real estate firms that cooperate with ICE, according to the Bronx Times.
## The Street Below

In Marble Hill, residents told amNY they fear another sweep. The protests after the shooting brought out the NYPD's Strategic Response Group, whose officers clashed with demonstrators, including incoming Upper Manhattan representative Darializa Avila Chevalier, who was shoved to the ground, amNY reported. Commissioner Jessica Tisch has said the NYPD did not assist federal agents.

sources.title: After Marble Hill shooting, Mamdani urges parking lot owners to keep ICE out
Bronx officials urge Marble Hill Target owners to ban ICE from parking lot after Oscar Belgal shooting

title: Powder in the Mail: Hazmat Crews Swarm Ritchie Torres' Bronx Office as Threats Hit New York Democrats
dek: An envelope with a suspicious powder exposed six people at Rep. Ritchie Torres' Fordham Road district office on Oct. 16, a day after suspicious mail targeted Sens. Chuck Schumer and Kirsten Gillibrand.
body: The envelope arrived at 540 East Fordham Road, the Bronx district office of Rep. Ritchie Torres, on Friday, Oct. 16. At 1:23 p.m., the FDNY got the call, according to amNY.

Inside was a suspicious powder. Six people were exposed, the FDNY said, and hazardous materials units were sent to the block between Lorillard Place and Bathgate Avenue, one of the busiest commercial strips in the borough.
## Non-Hazardous, This Time

Testing determined the substance was not hazardous, and an FDNY spokesperson reported no injuries, amNY reported. Torres' staff notified the FBI, NYPD and FDNY, and the envelope was turned over to the FBI. The investigation is ongoing.
Torres posted on X that his office had received an envelope containing a suspicious substance and that his team was shaken but would not be deterred from serving the 15th Congressional District.
> "The new normal." — Rep. Ritchie Torres, on threats against officials and staff
## A Pattern of Mailings

The Bronx scare came one day after suspicious mail targeted two of New York's most powerful Democrats. On Thursday, Oct. 15, suspicious mail was sent to Sen. Chuck Schumer and Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, amNY reported. The Washington Post reported that Schumer was among several senators whose offices were targeted. The U.S. Postal Inspection Service intercepted the mail bound for Gillibrand's New York City office, and Gillibrand thanked postal inspectors for protecting her staff.

The FBI and the Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings around the country, including letters sent to secretaries of state and election offices, some of which contained an unknown substance, according to amNY. The FBI declined to say whether the Torres envelope is connected to that investigation.
## Weeks Before the Vote

The timing is ominous. The mailings arrived as New York heads into the final stretch of a hard-fought governor's race between Gov. Kathy Hochul and Republican Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, with early voting about to begin and Election Day set for Nov. 3.

Election offices have been among the targets nationally, raising alarms for the workers who staff them. For the six people exposed on Fordham Road, the test results brought an all-clear. The FBI had not said by Oct. 16 who sent the envelope.

sources.title: Suspicious powder sent to Rep. Ritchie Torres' Bronx office in latest mail scare targeting New York Democratic pols
Hochul, Blakeman hit campaign trail before early voting underway

title: Mamdani Steps Into the Governor's Race, Calling Blakeman 'a Bad Apple'
dek: Gov. Kathy Hochul's campaign released a video on Oct. 15 featuring Mayor Zohran Mamdani attacking Republican Bruce Blakeman on Medicaid, child care and ICE, as both candidates closed out their pitches before early voting.
body: For most of the campaign, the question in Albany was whether New York City's democratic socialist mayor would help or hurt the governor. On Thursday, Oct. 15, Gov. Kathy Hochul's campaign answered by putting Mayor Zohran Mamdani in front of the camera, according to amNY.

The roughly one-minute video, also posted as an Instagram reel, argues that Republican nominee Bruce Blakeman, the Nassau County executive, would make life harder for working New Yorkers. It closes with Mamdani calling Blakeman a bad apple.
## Three Lines of Attack

The ad stitches together clips of Blakeman on three issues, amNY reported. On Medicaid, it includes an earlier clip of Blakeman saying the goal was to cut Medicaid in half, two days after he insisted during Tuesday's televised debate that he had never said he would do so.
> "I never said that I would cut Medicaid in half." — Bruce Blakeman, during the debate

On child care, the video revisits Blakeman's criticism of subsidized care for parents who are not working, including a remark in which he used a crude phrase to describe an unemployed parent receiving aid. On immigration, Mamdani says Blakeman would rather send money to ICE, over footage of Blakeman praising the agency's work, amNY reported. As Nassau County executive, Blakeman has cooperated with federal immigration authorities.
## Blakeman Fires Back

In a statement, Blakeman defended his child care remarks, saying he supports universal child care for working parents but questions paying for care for parents who do not work, amNY reported. He accused Hochul and Mamdani of making New York less affordable through taxes, utility costs and transit fares. He did not address the Medicaid clip.
## Asset or Liability

Speaking to reporters at an affordable housing event with Hochul in East New York, Mamdani said he expects to join the governor on the trail before Election Day on Nov. 3. Asked whether he helps or hurts her, he said he believes the work his administration is doing is an asset, amNY reported. He pointed to a $1.2 billion investment that opened 2,000 free child care seats for 2-year-olds this year, with 10,000 more expected next year.
## The Final Weekend Before Early Voting

By Sunday, Oct. 18, the candidates were working opposite ends of the region. Hochul campaigned in Concourse Village in the Bronx, highlighting the state's ban on cell phones in schools and expanded access to community college and child care, ABC7 New York reported. Local supporters told the station that turnout remains a major challenge for Democrats in the borough.
Hochul told the Bronx crowd she was counting on them.

Blakeman campaigned in Elmont on Long Island alongside Lee Zeldin, the former congressman whom Hochul narrowly defeated in 2022 and who later became administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency under President Trump. Blakeman argued that high costs are driving people out of the state and promised to cut taxes and utility rates. Hochul countered that New York has the fastest-growing economy in the country, ABC7 reported.
Early voting begins the following weekend.

sources.title: 2026 Governor's Race: Mamdani steps up role in Hochul campaign with new attack ad on 'bad apple' Blakeman
Governor Hochul, Bruce Blakeman hit campaign trail before early voting underway next weekend

title: 'Execution-Style': Rockaway Teen Charged With Murder of 14-Year-Old Over a Scooter
dek: A 17-year-old from Far Rockaway was held without bail on Oct. 14 after being charged with murder in the Sept. 21 shooting death of a 14-year-old boy at the Ocean Bay Apartments in Arverne.
body: The boy rolled into the courtyard of the Ocean Bay Apartments in Arverne on a push scooter, with three others, at about 3:33 p.m. on Monday, Sept. 21. Minutes later he was on the ground with a bullet in his back, according to Queens prosecutors as reported by QNS.

Three weeks after the killing, a 17-year-old from Far Rockaway walked into the 101st Precinct station house at about 11:30 a.m. on Tuesday, Oct. 13, and surrendered to detectives, QNS reported, citing a law enforcement source. He was booked on murder and weapons charges. He is not being named here because he is a minor.
## What Prosecutors Allege

According to the criminal complaint described by QNS, the teen approached the 14-year-old beside a residential building at 51-24 Beach Channel Drive and fired twice. One round struck the boy in the lower back and traveled to his heart.

Police said the encounter began as an attempted robbery and that the suspect pulled a handgun during a struggle, QNS reported. After the boy fell, prosecutors allege, the teen took the scooter and fled east on Norton Avenue, then changed clothes in a public bathroom. Investigators later recovered the clothing from a trash bin there, according to the complaint.
EMS rushed the boy to Cohen Children's Medical Center in Glen Oaks, where he underwent emergency surgery. He was pronounced dead at the hospital.
> "A targeted, execution-style killing." — Queens District Attorney Melinda Katz
Katz said that, as alleged, the victim was shot through his heart, QNS reported.
## In Court

The 17-year-old was arraigned on Wednesday, Oct. 14, in Queens Supreme Court on charges of second-degree murder and two counts of second-degree criminal possession of a weapon. Justice Seth Steed ordered him held without bail and set a return date of Oct. 19, according to QNS.
If convicted, he faces up to 25 years to life in prison. The charges are accusations, and he is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.
## A Peninsula's Grief

The killing struck one of the city's most isolated corners. The Ocean Bay Apartments, a sprawling public housing complex along Beach Channel Drive, sit at the far end of the Rockaway peninsula, where the A train and the ferry are the main lifelines to the rest of the city.

The case comes as the NYPD reports historically low gun violence. Through September, the department counted 203 murders citywide, the fewest on record for the first nine months of a year, ABC7 New York reported. For one Arverne family, those numbers offer no comfort.

title: City Hall Buys a Piece of the Quantum Future at 770 Broadway
dek: Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced on Oct. 14 a nearly $30 million city investment in an NYU quantum technology lab that gives the city 15% of revenue from inventions made with city-funded equipment.
body: New York has handed out tax breaks and capital grants to the technology industry for decades. On Wednesday, Oct. 14, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced a deal that asks for something back, according to amNY.

The city will put nearly $30 million into QFab, a quantum technology fabrication lab New York University plans to open in 2030 at 770 Broadway in Manhattan. In return, the city will receive 15% of the revenue NYU's central administration earns from technologies developed using city-funded equipment at the facility.
## A First for the City

City officials described the arrangement as unprecedented for New York, amNY reported. The city has taken equity stakes in smaller projects before but had never claimed a share of intellectual property revenue. If inventions built with the city's equipment are commercialized, New York could collect licensing fees, royalties and other proceeds. If they are not, it collects nothing.
> "Public subsidy is just put forward as an incentive." — Mayor Zohran Mamdani

Mamdani argued that cities should also share in the revenue such subsidies help create. He called it a model his administration had been excited about since its first day in office, though he did not commit to making revenue-sharing mandatory for future city-funded projects, amNY reported.
## The Money

The project carries roughly $284 million in combined backing. NYU President Linda Mills said the university is committing $255 million: $100 million in capital spending and $155 million in operating costs over the next decade. The city's share, nearly $29 million in capital funding, flows through the New York City Economic Development Corporation.
NYU projects about 2,000 permanent jobs and support for more than 100 companies.
## Inside QFab

The 23,000-square-foot lab will give researchers, students and companies access to specialized equipment for building and testing quantum devices, amNY reported. Quantum technology applies the physics of the very small to computing, communications and sensing, with potential uses in medicine and energy.

Under the agreement, the city gets three seats on QFab's executive advisory board, going to NYCEDC and two CUNY schools, Borough of Manhattan Community College and New York City College of Technology. The administration hopes the seats will push research toward sustainable technology, medical advances and more efficient energy systems.
## A Pipeline for CUNY

The deal also includes internships, summer workshops and certificate programs for CUNY and public school students. Juan de Pablo, executive dean of NYU's Tandon School of Engineering, said more than 3,000 CUNY students are expected to benefit, beginning at BMCC and City Tech before expanding across the system, amNY reported.

Whether the 15% stake ever produces a check depends on discoveries that have not been made yet in a building that will not open for four years. But the structure marks a shift in how City Hall wants to deal with the institutions it funds.

sources.title: NYC secures stake in potential tech revenue with $30M investment in NYU quantum lab

title: Mamdani Stands by Tisch as the Left Demands Her Head
dek: Mayor Zohran Mamdani said on Oct. 13 he has no plans to replace NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch, a day after ordering the department's first comprehensive use-of-force review in a decade.
body: Standing in Battery Park City on Tuesday, Oct. 13, after a ceremony that added 42 names to the NYPD's Memorial Wall of fallen officers, Mayor Zohran Mamdani gave his clearest answer yet to the activists who helped elect him and now want his police commissioner gone, according to ABC7 New York.
> "I have no plans to change that." — Mayor Zohran Mamdani
Mamdani credited Commissioner Jessica Tisch with uprooting corruption from the upper ranks of the NYPD while driving down crime across the city, the station reported.
## The Pressure From the Left

Some of the mayor's own supporters argue his policing changes do not go far enough. The Democratic Socialists of America have accused Tisch of helping Immigration and Customs Enforcement operate in New York, a charge both Tisch and Mamdani deny, ABC7 reported.

The group has tied that accusation to the Oct. 8 ICE shooting in Marble Hill, contending that federal agents were able to leave an Inwood hospital with the wounded man because NYPD Strategic Response Group officers cleared protesters from the street. One protester, Micaela Martinez, told the station that the NYPD is not making people feel safe at demonstrations.

Mamdani, once a sharp critic of the police, has appeared to moderate since taking office, ABC7 noted, though he has vowed to dismantle the Strategic Response Group and shift its focus to counterterrorism.
## A Review Ten Years Overdue

A day earlier, on Oct. 12, Mamdani directed the NYPD to carry out its first comprehensive review of use-of-force policies and practices in a decade, ABC7 reported. The review is to run over the coming months and include community engagement on how the rules are applied and whether they should change.

The order followed scrutiny of a case from Ozone Park, Queens. In May 2024, police called to a home where a 19-year-old was reportedly in a psychiatric crisis shot him after, police said, he lunged at officers with scissors. The state attorney general cleared the officers, but the Civilian Complaint Review Board later concluded they used excessive force. One officer retired before facing an administrative trial because the NYPD did not notify the board of his pending retirement; Tisch called the failure an oversight, ABC7 reported.

Alongside the review, the mayor announced stronger notification rules for pending retirements, more money for the inspector general who monitors the NYPD, and standardized public disclosure for police-involved incidents.
Mamdani said that when the government uses force against a New Yorker, the standard for accountability must be at its highest.
## Pushback From Both Sides

The reforms satisfied neither flank. The president of the Police Benevolent Association argued there should be no review of use-of-force rules without a matching look at how the CCRB interprets them, ABC7 reported. Detectives' Endowment Association President Scott Munro said the mayor should focus on the review board instead, arguing its staff are anti-police.
From the other direction, Loyda Colon of the Justice Committee said a broader overhaul of NYPD discipline is needed and called the measures far from enough.
The department also plans to review its response to the hospital protests that followed the Marble Hill shooting, according to ABC7.

sources.title: Mayor Zohran Mamdani says he has no plans to remove NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch
NYC to review NYPD use-of-force policies for first time in decade

title: Stabbed Over a Gold Chain, an Off-Duty Detective Chased His Attackers Five Blocks
dek: NYPD Detective Jose Mercedes, stabbed repeatedly during an attempted robbery in Norwood on Oct. 2, spoke publicly for the first time on Oct. 13 as two men arrested in Massachusetts faced charges in the Bronx.
body: Detective Jose Mercedes was on vacation. He was standing at the trunk of his car near East 206th Street and Rochambeau Avenue in Norwood, in the Bronx's 52nd Precinct, on Oct. 2 when two men on an e-bike came up behind him, according to ABC7 New York and amNY.
They wanted the gold chain around his neck, a gift from his mother, ABC7 reported. Mercedes, 33, fought back. He told them, in English and in Spanish, that he was a police officer.
> "They didn't care." — NYPD Detective Jose Mercedes
## The Wounds

Mercedes was stabbed seven times, according to amNY; ABC7 reported he was stabbed 10 times. He lost a significant amount of blood, ABC7 reported, yet according to his union he did not go down. Detectives' Endowment Association President Scott Munro said Mercedes chased the attackers for five blocks while bleeding.
He was taken to Jacobi Hospital and released on Oct. 4, amNY reported. He has not returned to work and is concentrating on regaining mobility in his left hand, according to ABC7.
## First Words in Public

On Tuesday, Oct. 13, Mercedes stood before cameras at DEA headquarters in Lower Manhattan, surrounded by colleagues who came to welcome him back, amNY reported. He told reporters he was happy to be alive and that he had never expected to be attacked while simply trying to enjoy his time off, ABC7 reported. He thanked fellow officers and federal partners for tracking down the suspects.
## A Manhunt That Ended in Lynn

Five days after the stabbing, the two men police accuse of carrying it out were arrested in Lynn, Massachusetts, by the New York–New Jersey Regional Fugitive Task Force and the U.S. Marshals, according to Munro, as reported by amNY. Munro identified them as D'Angelo Rafael Jean Caraballo and Sneider Mejia Bautista and said they face charges including attempted murder.

ABC7 described the two as undocumented Dominican nationals with lengthy criminal histories and reported that they had been extradited to New York and were expected to be arraigned in the Bronx on Wednesday, Oct. 14. The men have not been convicted, and the allegations against them have not been tested in court.

Munro, whose union has been feuding with the Civilian Complaint Review Board and City Hall over discipline, used the moment to call for long prison terms; a photo caption in amNY said he urged 25 years to life for the suspects.

The attack comes amid a run of violence against officers in the Bronx. On the evening of Saturday, Oct. 17, a uniformed officer responding to a loud music call near Garrison Avenue and Whittier Street in Hunts Point was struck by a white Honda SUV whose driver fled, ABC7 reported. The officer suffered a leg injury; no arrest had been announced.

sources.title: NYPD detective stabbed seven times reunites with colleagues after hospital release
NYPD detective stabbed in the Bronx during vacation shares story of survival
NYPD officer struck by hit-and-run driver while responding to loud music call, officials say

title: Chaos at 30,000 Feet: Selma Blair Taken Into Custody at JFK After Flight Attendants Report Attack
dek: Actress Selma Blair was taken into custody at JFK Airport on Oct. 11 after police were called about a physically abusive passenger on Delta Flight 938 from Los Angeles, and her representative blamed a medical emergency.
body: Delta Air Lines Flight 938 from Los Angeles was parked at the gate at John F. Kennedy International Airport at about 11 p.m. on Sunday, Oct. 11, when Port Authority police were called to deal with a physically abusive passenger, according to amNY.
The passenger was the actress Selma Blair, 54. She was taken into custody immediately and brought to a nearby hospital for evaluation, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey said.
## What Allegedly Happened

Accounts of the flight remain secondhand. Multiple reports cited by amNY said Blair bit a member of the crew and tried to open a door of the aircraft. Variety, citing TMZ, reported that she tried to open the door while the plane was in the air, punched one flight attendant and bit another.
Two flight attendants reported injuries, and one was taken to a hospital for further evaluation, amNY reported.

The Port Authority said the FBI is investigating, which is standard when alleged crimes occur aboard an aircraft in flight. As of amNY's report on Oct. 12, it was not clear what charges, if any, Blair would face or whether she had appeared in court. The allegations have not been proven.
## 'A Medical Emergency'
A representative for Blair told Variety that a medical emergency led to the incident. The representative said she received immediate medical attention after landing and was in stable condition.

Blair, known for films including Cruel Intentions and Legally Blonde, has spoken publicly for years about living with multiple sclerosis. Her representative did not specify the nature of the emergency on the flight, according to the reports.
## The Airline
A Delta spokesperson told amNY the incident had no operational impact and that the flight landed ahead of schedule.
> "Delta has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior." — Delta spokesperson
The spokesperson added that the safety of customers and crew always comes first.

Assaults on flight crews have become a recurring concern for the airline industry, and federal law treats interference with flight crew members as a serious offense. Whether the case moves forward will depend on what investigators conclude about the events in the cabin and the medical circumstances Blair's camp has described.

sources.title: Actress Selma Blair arrested at JFK following violent attack on board Delta Air Lines flight

title: Anyone With a Guitar: Strawberry Fields Becomes an All-Day Beatles Jam on John Lennon's Birthday
dek: Hundreds of fans and dozens of musicians gathered at Strawberry Fields in Central Park on Oct. 9 for an all-day jam session marking John Lennon's birthday, amNY reported.
body: No one was booked. That was the point. On Friday, Oct. 9, the day John Lennon would have turned 86, hundreds of Beatles fans and dozens of musicians gathered around the Imagine mosaic at Strawberry Fields in Central Park to sing, dance and leave flowers, according to amNY.
David Muniz, who keeps the list of performers at the memorial, told amNY that nobody had a set slot, so anyone could play.
> "Anybody can come here and play today." — David Muniz
The day was billed as an all-day Lennon jam at a site amNY described as already recognized by Guinness World Records for a music marathon. It was expected to run until about 10 p.m.
## The Core Seven

At the front of the circle sat the Core Seven, a group of key musicians, several of them from Queens, who led the marathon from one Beatles song to the next, amNY reported. Jamie Rivera, one of them, sang "Eight Days a Week" and said anyone with a guitar can show up. Drummer Michael Naimoli, who also plays in the cover band Yesterday and Today, kept time.

The songbook ran through "Eight Days a Week," "A Hard Day's Night," "Good Day Sunshine," "Here Comes the Sun" and "Help!" The Beatles recorded 213 songs, 188 originals and 25 covers, amNY noted, so there was no danger of running out.
## Pilgrims

The crowd mixed regulars and first-timers, some from out of state and abroad. Francisco Rodriguez and Luis Ramirez traveled from Mexico to play guitar at the memorial, according to amNY. Alec Lobel of North Bergen, New Jersey, said he has been coming for a long time. Tommy Behnke, an Upper West Side resident, said he had grown up with the band from his first day.
Billy Flood, a Brooklyn musician who plays in Weekend Cinema, told amNY that he comes twice a year, for Lennon's birthday and for the memorial on the anniversary of his death.
## Two Days a Year

Lennon was born on Oct. 9, 1940, and was shot and killed on Dec. 8, 1980, outside the Dakota on Central Park West, a short walk from the spot where fans now gather. Muniz said crowds are large on both dates, but that the birthday is the happier one.
For those who cannot wait until December, Bill Purdy pointed to Beatles and Sixties jam sessions held on the first Saturday of each month at the Fish Bar in the East Village, amNY reported.

sources.title: Beatles fans flock to Strawberry Fields, celebrating John Lennon's birthday

title: Seven Shots Through a Windshield: ICE Agent Wounds Driver in Marble Hill as His Son Sits in Back
dek: A federal immigration officer shot a 28-year-old man in the neck during an ICE operation in Marble Hill on Oct. 8, and the man was later taken into ICE custody despite the mayor's calls to the White House.
body: It was about 4 p.m. on a Thursday, the hour when children spill out of school onto the streets of Marble Hill, when a federal immigration agent opened fire on a Honda CR-V near Marble Hill Avenue and West 225th Street on Oct. 8, according to ABC7 New York.

The rounds went through the front windshield. The 28-year-old man behind the wheel was struck in the neck, just below his left ear. In the back seat sat a 5-year-old boy believed to be his son. The child was not physically hurt, and NYPD officers later found him safe with a family member, the station reported.
## Seven Rounds

NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said at least one officer fired seven times, ABC7 reported. Witnesses described chaos on crowded sidewalks. One told the station they heard seven or eight shots; another said the shooter fired without knowing a child was in the car. Witnesses said the boy appeared frozen with fear. About 90 minutes after the gunfire, dozens of ICE agents were seen leaving the area.
The man was taken to NewYork-Presbyterian Allen Hospital in Inwood, where Tisch said he was in stable condition.
## Two Accounts

The Department of Homeland Security said its officers were carrying out a targeted operation to arrest a Dominican national with a prior grand larceny conviction and several earlier arrests, and said he had ties to the Trinitarios gang, ABC7 reported. ICE also said the man had been arrested by the NYPD on Dec. 7, 2023, and released a few days later.

According to ABC7, the operation was connected to an investigation into people with ties to the migrants involved in the July 2025 shooting of an off-duty federal officer in Fort Washington Park. Two Dominican nationals in that case were sentenced in federal court the same week; state charges remain pending. None of the allegations against the wounded man had been tested in court as of the reports.
Public Advocate Jumaane Williams pushed back on efforts to portray the man negatively, describing him as a father picking up his child who was shot by a federal agency, ABC7 reported.
## A Hospital Under Siege

By Thursday evening, hundreds of protesters had gathered outside the Inwood hospital, according to ABC7. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at a news conference shortly before midnight that he had spent hours on the phone with President Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin trying to secure the man's release. Those efforts failed, and the mayor later said the man had been taken into ICE custody.
> "We will not normalize ICE's viciousness." — Mayor Zohran Mamdani

Mamdani called the shooting an outrage and said ICE is an agency that must be abolished. Gov. Kathy Hochul demanded full transparency from federal authorities, urged a halt to ICE enforcement operations in New York and called for the release of body camera footage, ABC7 reported. Bronx Borough President Vanessa Gibson and Council Member Carmen De La Rosa also condemned the operation.
## Behind Federal Walls

The wounded man ended up at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, held in a segregated unit, according to a 58-page habeas corpus petition filed by the Legal Aid Society and reported by amNY on Oct. 14. The petition says a bullet remains lodged in his neck, that the left side of his face is numb and his hearing on that side is impaired, and that he had received only ibuprofen with no word on surgery doctors had recommended.

His lawyers allege the agents never identified themselves or showed a warrant before firing, and that ICE did not prepare a Notice to Appear until the next day. The Federal Bureau of Prisons told amNY it does not deny any inmate necessary medical treatment. DHS said the shooting is under investigation by Homeland Security Investigations and the FBI.

U.S. District Judge Hector Gonzalez barred the government from deporting the man or moving him outside the city's two federal judicial districts, and ordered the administration to explain by 10 a.m. on Oct. 19 why he should not be released immediately, amNY reported. His attorneys say he denies any gang involvement and that ICE has offered no evidence of it; DHS said he will remain in custody pending removal proceedings.
## The Fallout Reaches the NYPD

The shooting quickly became a test for City Hall. The Democratic Socialists of America later argued that the agents were able to leave the hospital with the wounded man because NYPD Strategic Response Group officers cleared protesters from the street, ABC7 reported on Oct. 13. Tisch and Mamdani have both denied that the NYPD is helping ICE carry out enforcement in the city, and the department said it would review its response to the hospital protests.

title: After Dark at Blood Manor, Manhattan's Largest Haunted House Opens Its Doors to Would-Be Monsters
dek: Blood Manor, billed as New York's largest haunted attraction, runs through Nov. 7 and this season offers a $350 Scare Actor Academy that lets guests become performers, amNY reported.
body: The line forms after nightfall, and the screaming starts inside. Blood Manor, billed as New York's largest haunted attraction, is back in Manhattan for the 2026 season, drawing thousands of guests through a landmarked building where the owner says the landlord has been supportive, according to amNY.
The attraction runs through Nov. 7. General admission starts at $50, with student discounts on specific days, and tickets are sold online, amNY reported.
## The Faces in the Dark
Jim Lorenzo, the owner and creator, told amNY that Blood Manor will stay at its current location as long as the lease allows.
> "We try to keep a location for as long as we possibly can." — Jim Lorenzo, Blood Manor

Some of the performers have been at it for years. Sammy Mena, known to regulars as the Blood Manor Clown, has been frightening guests there since 2006. Another performer, Yum Yum, guards the entrance. Mena told amNY that the cast likes to torment everyone who waits outside.

The cast is the heart of the house. Mena, who has worked Blood Manor since 2006, is one of its longest-serving performers, and his routine begins before guests ever reach the door, aimed at the people waiting in line, according to amNY.
## Become the Monster

This year Blood Manor added a new way in. Its Scare Actor Academy lets guests cross to the other side of the fright and work as scare actors themselves. The $350 ticket includes a professional costume and makeup, and one of the instructors is a performer known as the Countess, according to amNY.
Lorenzo told the publication that his favorite thing about this year's house is the same thing that has been his favorite every year.
## A Night for a Cause

On Oct. 27, Blood Manor will hold its fourth annual charity event in collaboration with Z100. The night honors Lorenzo's son, Joey, who died of cancer six years ago, and donations go to St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, amNY reported.
## Planning a Visit

Tickets are sold online, with general admission from $50 and student discounts on select days. The season ends Nov. 7, a week after Halloween, and Lorenzo expects attendance in line with past years, when the house drew thousands of guests, amNY reported.

sources.title: Behind the screams and squirms of Blood Manor, New York's largest haunted attraction

title: Fifteen Floors: Bronx Mother Killed, Infant Daughter Survives After Police Say Both Were Pushed From a Balcony
dek: A 23-year-old woman died and her 8-month-old daughter was critically injured after police say both were pushed from a 15th-floor balcony in Allerton on Oct. 6, and the NYPD is seeking the child's father.
body: The call came in around 3:30 a.m. on Tuesday, Oct. 6. Outside the Allerville Arms, an apartment tower on Olinville Avenue in the Allerton section of the Bronx, officers found a 23-year-old woman and her 8-month-old daughter on the ground, according to ABC7 New York.
Police say both had been pushed from a 15th-floor balcony.
## A Race to Jacobi
Officers did not wait for an ambulance. They put the baby in a patrol car and rushed her to Jacobi Hospital, ABC7 reported. The mother was also taken to the hospital, where she was pronounced dead.

The infant survived the fall. By Wednesday, Oct. 7, she was in critical but stable condition, and police said they believed she would live. Investigators told the station they believe the mother fell in a way that cushioned the impact for her daughter.
## The Search

The NYPD said the woman's death is being investigated as a homicide. Detectives are seeking a 31-year-old man believed to be her ex-boyfriend and the child's father, and released his photo, ABC7 reported. Authorities said surveillance video captured him leaving the building. As of the station's Oct. 8 update, no arrest had been announced, and he has not been charged with a crime.
Investigators are still working to determine what happened inside the apartment in the hours before dawn.
## Warnings Before the Fall

Sources told Eyewitness News there was a documented history of domestic violence at the apartment, and that police had responded there twice in January. A neighbor told the station that earlier this year they saw a man trying to kick in the apartment door.

Stephanie McGraw, founder and chief executive of the Harlem domestic violence organization WARM, told ABC7 that the woman was one of roughly seven women killed in New York City over the past two months.

The killing came during what the NYPD calls a historic year for public safety, with murders through September at their lowest level on record. But domestic violence has long been among the hardest crimes for police to prevent, often unfolding behind closed doors where earlier calls for help leave a trail investigators can only follow afterward.
Anyone with information is asked to contact NYPD Crime Stoppers at 1-800-577-TIPS. People experiencing domestic violence in New York City can reach the city's 24-hour hotline at 1-800-621-HOPE.

sources.title: NYPD releases photo of man wanted in connection to deadly balcony shove in the Bronx
NYPD says shootings and murders reached record lows through September

title: The Quietest Guns on Record: NYC Shootings and Murders Hit Historic Lows Through September
dek: The NYPD said on Oct. 6 that the city recorded 489 shooting incidents and 203 murders in the first nine months of 2026, the lowest totals for that period in its records.
body: For decades, the numbers that defined New York City were measured in bodies. On Tuesday, Oct. 6, the NYPD released a set that would have been unthinkable a generation ago, according to ABC7 New York.

From January through September, the city recorded 489 shooting incidents, 594 shooting victims and 203 murders. Each figure is the lowest for the first nine months of any year in the department's records. Compared with the same stretch of 2021, 846 fewer people were shot.
> "The fewest shooting incidents, shooting victims, and murders." — NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch
Tisch said the totals were the lowest for the first nine months of any year in recorded history, ABC7 reported.
## Every Borough Down

Major crime fell 6.6% citywide, from 92,057 reported incidents to 86,023, and dropped in all five boroughs. The Bronx, long the epicenter of the city's gun violence, posted the steepest decline at 11.9%, according to the NYPD figures.

The third quarter alone was historic. From July through September, the city logged 167 shooting incidents, 213 shooting victims and 73 murders, each the lowest on record for that quarter, as major crime fell 9.4%.

Robbery was down 12.2%, burglary 13.7%, grand larceny 5.8% and auto theft 12.4%. In public housing, murders, shootings, shooting victims and robberies all reached record lows for the first nine months, and major crime fell 6.5%, ABC7 reported.
## Where It Rose

Not every line moved in the right direction. Felony assaults ticked up 0.2%. Reported rapes rose 3.7%, which police said partly reflects recent reports of incidents from previous years. Confirmed hate crimes rose 12.9%, and more than half were anti-Jewish, according to the department.

Transit crime was roughly flat, up 0.9%. The NYPD said 2026 ranks among the safest years in the subway in 15 years, excluding the pandemic-era ridership collapse, and Tisch vowed to go after the people driving violence underground.
## Credit and Caveats

Police credited gun seizures, gang takedowns and data-driven deployments. Mayor Zohran Mamdani credited both officers and violence-prevention programs and noted that major crime fell in every borough, ABC7 reported.

The figures arrive at a politically delicate moment for the mayor, who is resisting pressure from parts of his own coalition to replace Tisch. Days after the release, a fatal shooting on a Midtown E train platform on Oct. 17 underscored how quickly a single act of violence can shake riders' confidence, regardless of what the year-to-date numbers say.

title: No Riot This Time: John Lydon Brings Public Image Ltd Back to the Old Ritz
dek: John Lydon and Public Image Ltd played a sold-out show at Webster Hall, the East Village room that was once the Ritz, where a 1981 PiL performance ended in a riot, The Villager reported on Oct. 7.
body: In 1981, Public Image Ltd played the Ritz on East 11th Street and the night ended in a riot. Instead of a conventional set, the crowd got projected shadows and recordings, and it tore at the room in protest, according to a review by Bob Krasner in The Villager, published by amNY.
Forty-five years later, the building is Webster Hall again, and John Lydon, the man the world first met as Johnny Rotten, came back to it. This time, Krasner wrote, nobody asked for their money back.
## The Lineup

The show was sold out. Lydon remains the only original member of PiL, the band he formed after the Sex Pistols collapsed. On stage with him were Lu Edmonds on guitar, Scott Firth on bass and Mark Roberts on drums, according to the review. The California punk band Plague Vendor opened with what Krasner described as a high-energy set.
## The Set

The band reached back to Metal Box, the 1979 record that remains PiL's defining statement, for "Poptones" and "Death Disco." They played "This Is Not a Love Song" and "Open Up," Lydon's 1993 collaboration with the electronic group Leftfield. The main set closed with a medley of "Rise" and "Religion," with the crowd chanting along, Krasner reported.

Lydon worked from a music stand holding his lyrics. He danced a bit, which the reviewer called the only surprising thing he did all night. Before the encore, he politely asked the audience whether they minded a three-minute break. At one point he blew his nose into a handkerchief and threw it into the crowd, which Krasner labeled the snottiest moment of the show.
## The Verdict
The reviewer was not entirely won over.
> "The music... tended to all sound the same after awhile." — Bob Krasner, The Villager

He granted that it was well played. Online reactions from fans ranged from awesome to glorious, according to the review, while at least one wrote that they would not have minded a riot. Some fans paid $80 for hoodies at the merchandise table.

For a city that once took its punk with broken glass, it was a strangely civil evening in the East Village. The provocateur who sneered his way through the 1970s is now a working musician who reads his words off a stand and checks with the audience before taking a break. The songs, at least, still carry the menace.

sources.title: John Lydon, aka Johnny Rotten, brings the noise to Webster Hall, but thankfully skips the riot
